title: Intent Classification — Core Method
description: The first job of a query interpreter is deciding what the user wants: a lookup, a comparison, a count, a list, or an explanation. A rule-based intent classifier matches the question against weighted keyword patterns — 'how many' signals a count, 'compare' signals a comparison — and picks the highest-scoring intent. Rules are transparent and debuggable, which matters when a misclassified intent sends the whole search down the wrong path. Production systems often start with rules exactly like these before graduating to trained models. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Slot Filling — Core Method
description: Once the intent is known, the interpreter extracts the slots: the named entities, dates, quantities, and filters the structured query needs. Regular expressions pull out years, quoted phrases, and numeric ranges, while gazetteers match known collection and field names. Each filled slot is reported with the span of text it came from, so a wrong extraction can be traced back to the exact words. Slot filling turns 'specs about caching from 2021' into field='specs', topic='caching', year=2021 without guesswork. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
demo:
import re
def slots(q):
    s = {}
    m = re.search(r"\b(19|20)\d{2}\b", q); s["year"] = m.group(0) if m else None
    s["phrases"] = re.findall(r'"([^"]+)"', q)
    m = re.search(r"(\d+)\s*-\s*(\d+)", q); s["range"] = m.groups() if m else None
    return s
print(slots('specs about "deep search" from 2021, ids 100-200'))

title: Template Compilation — Core Method
description: Interpreted questions compile into structured queries through templates: one template per intent, with slots plugged into field filters, sort orders, and result limits. The compiler validates every template instance — unknown fields rejected, type mismatches caught — before anything touches the archive. Because the structured query is a plain data structure, it can be logged, cached, and re-run exactly. This compilation step is the bridge between human language and the machine-readable queries archives actually execute. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Synonym Expansion — Core Method
description: Users rarely use the archive's exact vocabulary, so the interpreter expands query terms through a synonym and alias map: 'find' and 'locate' both become the lookup operator, 'AI' expands to 'artificial intelligence'. Expansions are marked as derived rather than original, so downstream ranking can weight exact matches above expanded ones. The alias map is curated from the archive's own vocabulary, which keeps expansions grounded in terms that actually appear. This closes the vocabulary gap that sinks so many natural-language searches. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Ambiguity Scoring — Core Method
description: Some questions parse two ways — 'show me Java records' could mean the island, the coffee, or the language — so the interpreter scores every candidate parse and only proceeds when the winner is clearly ahead. When the top two parses score within a threshold, the system asks a targeted clarification question instead of guessing. Each parse's score combines intent confidence, slot coverage, and vocabulary fit, and the full score breakdown is kept for audit. Asking one good question beats returning a confident wrong answer. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
demo:
parses = [("island", 0.62), ("language", 0.58), ("coffee", 0.21)]
parses.sort(key=lambda p: -p[1])
top, second = parses[0], parses[1]
if top[1] - second[1] < 0.10:
    print("ambiguous: did you mean '%s' or '%s'?" % (top[0], second[0]))
else:
    print("proceeding with:", top[0])
